concepts.title: Prompt Engineering Principles: Specificity, Examples, and Structure
concepts.description: Prompt engineering is applied conditioning -- specificity, well-chosen few-shot examples, and explicit output structure all work by narrowing the space of plausible next-token continuations toward the behavior you actually want, not by being more polite or more verbose.
learningObjectives: Explain, in terms of the next-token-prediction mechanism, why vague prompts produce inconsistent output across repeated calls.
Apply specificity techniques -- explicit role, constraints, format, and things to avoid -- to reliably tighten a prompt's behavior.
Design effective few-shot examples and explain both why they work and the biased-example pitfall that undermines them.
Request structured output (e.g. JSON matching a schema) reliably, and defensively handle the cases where it still isn't valid.
Diagnose a poorly-performing prompt and identify which principle -- specificity, examples, or structure -- is being violated.

sections.heading: Specificity: Why Vague Prompts Produce Inconsistent Output
sections.body:
Every word in a prompt conditions the probability distribution over what comes next -- that's the entire mechanism covered in the previous module, and prompt engineering is really just the practical craft of exploiting that fact on purpose. A vague prompt like 'write about dogs' leaves an enormous amount of the distribution unconstrained: genre, length, tone, structure, and level of detail are all left wide open, which means the 'most probable continuation' itself varies a great deal from call to call, because there are many, many genuinely plausible continuations of that exact same four-word prompt.

Specificity isn't about being thorough or polite for its own sake -- it's about mechanically narrowing that space. Compare 'write about dogs' with 'write a 150-word paragraph for a veterinary clinic's blog, aimed at first-time dog owners, explaining why puppies need multiple rounds of vaccinations rather than just one, in a warm but not overly cute tone, and without using bullet points.' Every clause in the second version removes a huge swath of otherwise-plausible continuations -- length, audience, topic angle, tone, and format are all pinned down -- so the range of outputs the model can plausibly produce shrinks dramatically, and different calls to the same specific prompt tend to converge on similar, reliable results.

A useful habit: whenever a prompt's output is inconsistent across runs or doesn't match what you wanted, ask specifically which dimension was left unconstrained -- length? audience? format? tone? things to exclude? -- rather than vaguely 'improving' the wording. Underspecification, not model unreliability, is the most common root cause of inconsistent prompt behavior.

sections.heading: Few-Shot Examples: Showing Instead of Telling
sections.body:
**Few-shot prompting** means including a small number of example input/output pairs directly in the prompt before the actual new input, letting the model infer the desired pattern from those examples rather than (or in addition to) a written instruction. This works for the same underlying reason instructions work: the examples become part of 'everything written so far' that conditions generation, and pattern-completion is precisely the mechanism the model is built on -- given several examples that consistently follow a pattern, the highest-probability continuation for a new, similar input is to follow that same pattern.

```python
prompt = '''Classify the sentiment of each review as positive, negative, or neutral.

Review: "This blender broke after two uses."
Sentiment: negative

Review: "Works exactly as described, very happy with it."
Sentiment: positive

Review: "It's fine, does what it says, nothing special."
Sentiment: neutral

Review: "Fast shipping but the product itself is mediocre."
Sentiment:'''
```

Few-shot examples earn their cost -- and they do cost real context-window tokens on every single call -- particularly when the desired output format or edge-case handling is hard to specify precisely in words but easy to demonstrate (an unusual output schema, a subtle tone, a tricky classification boundary between two similar categories). They tend to add less value for tasks the model already handles reliably zero-shot, where the extra tokens mostly add cost and context-budget pressure without changing behavior much.

The most common pitfall is **unrepresentative examples**: if every example you provide happens to share some accidental property (all three sentiment examples above skew toward short reviews, or in a worse case, all three happen to be non-negative), the model can latch onto that accidental pattern rather than the actual rule you intended, and mishandle new inputs that don't share it. Order can matter too, and the token cost is recurring, not one-time -- both are worth weighing against how much a given task genuinely benefits from demonstration versus instruction alone.

sections.heading: Requesting Structured Output Reliably
Putting It Together: A Layered Prompt
sections.body:
Production-grade prompts are rarely a single sentence -- they typically layer several of these techniques deliberately: a role or system-level instruction that sets overall behavior and tone; the specific task and its constraints, stated explicitly; the desired output schema or format, ideally with a concrete example of it; and, when the task benefits from demonstration, one or a few few-shot examples showing the pattern in action, usually placed closest to the actual new input since content nearer the point of generation tends to exert the most direct influence on it.

The most common bug in layered prompts is an internal contradiction across layers that the author never notices because each layer, read in isolation, looks fine: a system prompt that says 'always respond in formal English,' paired with a few-shot example that happens to be in a casual tone or a different language, leaves the model with genuinely conflicting conditioning signals about which pattern to actually follow, and the result is often an unpredictable blend of both, or an inconsistent choice between them across different calls. Whenever a layered prompt behaves erratically, it's worth explicitly checking every layer against every other layer for this kind of unintentional conflict before assuming the model is simply being unreliable.

examples.title: Specificity Turns a Vague Prompt Into a Reliable One
examples.code:
vague_prompt = "Write about dogs."

specific_prompt = (
    "Write a 150-word paragraph for a veterinary clinic's blog, aimed at "
    "first-time dog owners, explaining why puppies need multiple rounds of "
    "vaccinations rather than just one. Use a warm but professional tone. "
    "Do not use bullet points or headings -- plain prose only."
)
examples.explanation: Both prompts are grammatically complete instructions, but they occupy very different amounts of 'possibility space.' The vague version leaves topic angle, audience, length, tone, and format all unconstrained, so the model's highest-probability continuation genuinely varies a lot between calls -- one run might produce a breed-comparison listicle, another a personal essay about dog ownership, another a set of fun facts. The specific version pins down every one of those dimensions explicitly, which narrows what counts as a plausible continuation down to a much smaller, much more consistent range of outputs. Nothing about the model changed between the two calls -- only how much of the output space the prompt itself left open.

examples.title: Few-Shot Prompting for a Custom Output Style, and the Biased-Example Trap
examples.explanation: The two examples teach the model a pattern purely by demonstration: take a plain product description and rewrite it with exclamation points, superlatives, and a direct-address 'your new favorite' framing -- nowhere does the prompt state that rule in words, and it doesn't need to, because the model infers it from the consistent pattern across both examples. The risk sits in exactly how those examples were chosen: both happen to be pleasant, everyday household items rewritten positively. If a new input were something the pattern doesn't obviously fit -- a product with a genuine downside, or a category unlike either example -- the model has no demonstrated precedent for how the intended pattern should handle that case, and might either force an inappropriately enthusiastic tone onto something that shouldn't get one, or handle it inconsistently across repeated calls. Good few-shot sets deliberately include examples that span the range of cases you actually expect, not just the easy, representative-looking ones that were convenient to write.

examples.title: Structured Output With Defensive Parsing and a Retry Loop
examples.explanation: Even with `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` -- a genuine constrained-decoding feature, not just a plain-text instruction -- the code still wraps the parse in a try/except rather than assuming success, because 'syntactically valid JSON' and 'exactly the schema and values you need' are two different guarantees, and providers' constrained-decoding features typically only guarantee the former. The retry loop is the more interesting part: rather than just failing immediately, it feeds the malformed output and the specific parser error message back into the conversation and asks the model to correct it, which works because the error message itself becomes useful conditioning context for the next generation attempt -- the model can often see exactly what went wrong (an unescaped quote, a trailing comma) and fix it, in a way that a generic 'try again' retry with no error detail usually can't. Capping retries and raising a clear exception after exhausting them prevents this from silently looping or silently returning bad data to the rest of the system.

misconceptions.description: Being more polite, more verbose, or adding a longer preamble to a prompt ('please', extended context-setting, flattery) makes the model perform noticeably better.
misconceptions.clarification: What actually improves reliability is narrowing the space of plausible continuations through concrete specificity -- explicit constraints, format, audience, examples -- not politeness or volume of text for its own sake. Padding a prompt with pleasantries or unnecessary preamble adds tokens (which cost money and context budget) without meaningfully constraining the output space, and can occasionally dilute the signal by burying the actually-important constraints among filler. The lever that matters is precision of constraint, not tone or length.

misconceptions.description: If you instruct the model to 'return valid JSON matching this schema,' you can trust that the returned string will always be parseable JSON that matches your schema.
misconceptions.clarification: A plain-text instruction to return JSON is just more conditioning, the same as any other instruction -- it strongly influences the output but doesn't hard-constrain it, so the model can still produce malformed JSON, extra prose around it, markdown code fences, or fields not in your schema. Genuine reliability requires either a real constrained-decoding feature (JSON mode, structured outputs, function/tool calling) that restricts which tokens are eligible at each generation step, or defensive parsing with a validate-and-retry loop on your side -- ideally both, since even constrained-decoding features typically guarantee valid syntax without guaranteeing your exact schema or correct values.

exercises.prompt: This function asks the model to return JSON and then parses it directly. It works in some test calls but throws json.JSONDecodeError intermittently in production. Find the likely cause and fix the parsing so it handles the model's actual output reliably.
exercises.code:
import json

def get_extracted_fields(prompt, client):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt + "\n\nReturn the result as JSON."}],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)   # fails intermittently
hints: A plain-text instruction to 'return the result as JSON' doesn't hard-constrain the output -- what else might the model wrap around the actual JSON, especially in a chat-style response?

Try printing `raw` the next time this fails -- models frequently wrap JSON in a markdown code fence (```json ... ```) or add a short sentence before or after it, especially without a more explicit format instruction.

Consider two complementary fixes: stripping markdown fences/extra text before parsing, and using a genuine JSON-mode / structured-output API parameter instead of relying on the instruction text alone.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code relies entirely on a plain-text instruction ('Return the result as JSON') to shape the output, with no hard constraint enforcing it and no defensive handling of the response -- so on the calls where the model wraps the JSON in a markdown code fence or adds a short leading/trailing sentence (both common, unpredictable behaviors for a chat-tuned model responding conversationally), `json.loads` receives text that isn't pure JSON and throws. The fix does two independent things: it switches to a genuine structured-output API parameter (`response_format`) that constrains which tokens the model can generate to ones forming valid JSON syntax, which is a meaningfully stronger guarantee than instruction text alone; and it defensively strips common wrapping artifacts (markdown fences) before parsing, with a clear, informative exception if parsing still fails, rather than letting a raw `JSONDecodeError` propagate with no context about what the model actually returned.

exercises.prompt: A few-shot sentiment classifier is built with three example reviews, and all three happen to be positive or neutral -- none are negative. Predict what's likely to happen when a clearly negative new review is classified, and explain why, in terms of what few-shot prompting actually does.
exercises.code:
prompt = '''Classify the sentiment of each review as positive, negative, or neutral.

Review: "Absolutely love this, best purchase this year!"
Sentiment: positive

Review: "It's okay, does the job."
Sentiment: neutral

Review: "Pretty good quality for the price."
Sentiment: positive

Review: "This is the worst product I have ever bought, complete waste of money."
Sentiment:'''
hints: Few-shot prompting works by pattern completion -- the model infers a pattern from the examples it's shown, not from a rule stated anywhere in words.
All three demonstrated examples land on positive or neutral. Has the prompt actually shown the model what a negative example, or the boundary into negative territory, looks like?
Consider: is it more likely the model correctly generalizes to a category it was never shown an example of, or that it's biased toward the labels it has seen repeatedly?
exercises.expectedAnswer: There's a real, elevated risk of misclassification -- the model may label the clearly negative review as neutral or even positive, or handle it inconsistently across repeated calls, because none of the three demonstrated examples showed what a negative classification actually looks like in this specific pattern. The prompt has strongly demonstrated positive and neutral but has given the model no in-context precedent for negative at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Few-shot prompting conditions the model on the specific pattern shown in the examples, and the model has no independent, rule-based understanding of 'positive/negative/neutral' beyond what's demonstrated in this exact prompt plus whatever it learned about sentiment generally during training. Because every example here reinforces positive or neutral outcomes, the in-context pattern is skewed, and the strongly negative new review is the first case in the prompt with no directly analogous demonstrated example -- the model has to fall back on general world knowledge about sentiment rather than the specific pattern this prompt establishes, which can produce inconsistent or miscalibrated results, especially for borderline cases. The fix is to include at least one clearly negative example in the few-shot set, ideally one that's unambiguous, so the demonstrated pattern actually spans the full range of labels the task requires, rather than accidentally training the in-context pattern toward only two of the three categories.

assessments.prompt: A prompt asks a model to 'return the extracted fields as JSON.' Which statement about the reliability of this instruction is most accurate?
options: It's a hard guarantee -- the API will refuse to return anything other than valid JSON once JSON is explicitly requested in the instructions.

It's just additional conditioning text like any other instruction; the model can still return malformed JSON, extra prose, or markdown fences unless a genuine structured-output feature or defensive parsing is also used.
It only works if the prompt also includes at least five few-shot examples of valid JSON output.
JSON requests are handled by a separate, non-generative subsystem that validates syntax before the response is returned to you.
assessments.explanation: A plain-text instruction to return JSON influences generation the same way any other instruction does -- by conditioning the probability distribution -- but it doesn't hard-constrain which tokens can be produced, so malformed output, wrapping prose, or markdown fences remain possible. Reliability comes from combining this with a real constrained-decoding feature (JSON mode / structured outputs / function calling) and defensive parsing on the calling side. Option A overstates what plain instructions guarantee. Option C is false -- while examples can help, there's no fixed minimum count required, and examples alone still don't hard-constrain output. Option D is wrong because there is no separate validating subsystem sitting between generation and the response by default; any validation has to be added explicitly, either via a provider's structured-output feature or your own code.

assessments.prompt: A colleague's prompt for extracting structured data from support tickets works reliably in testing but occasionally returns invalid or incomplete JSON in production, at low but nonzero frequency. Explain the likely underlying causes and how you'd make the pipeline robust against this, rather than just hoping it stops happening.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core issue is that a chat-tuned model generating JSON is still doing ordinary next-token generation, not executing a hard syntax-checked serialization routine -- so 'usually correct' rather than 'always correct' is the expected baseline behavior for JSON produced from a plain-text instruction alone, and low-frequency failures are exactly what that predicts: an occasional wrapped code fence, a dropped closing brace, a hallucinated or missing field, a number rendered as a quoted string. Testing often under-samples this because manual testing tends to reuse a small number of representative inputs, while production traffic eventually surfaces the wider range of ticket content -- unusual characters, unusually long text, edge-case categories -- that's more likely to trigger a rarer failure mode. Making the pipeline genuinely robust means not relying on the instruction text as the only safeguard: first, switch to a real constrained-decoding feature if the provider offers one (JSON mode, structured outputs, or function/tool calling), which restricts the model to only emit syntactically valid JSON tokens rather than merely being told to; second, always parse defensively downstream, wrapping the parse in error handling rather than assuming success, and stripping common wrapping artifacts like markdown fences before parsing; third, validate the parsed result against your actual required schema (right fields present, right types), not just against 'is this valid JSON at all,' since syntactically valid JSON can still be missing required data; and fourth, build in a bounded retry path that feeds the specific parsing or validation error back to the model and asks it to correct that exact problem, since a targeted retry with the actual error message tends to succeed far more often than either giving up immediately or retrying blindly with no feedback. None of this makes failures literally impossible, but it converts a rare unhandled crash into a monitored, recoverable, and measurable failure rate.

concepts.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, End to End
concepts.description: RAG solves the two hardest problems of relying purely on a model's trained-in knowledge -- information that's stale, private, or simply never seen, and answers that can't be traced back to a source -- by retrieving relevant text at query time and feeding it into the context window as grounding for generation.
learningObjectives: Describe the end-to-end RAG pipeline: chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, augmentation, and generation, and what each stage is responsible for.
Explain the chunk-size tradeoff between retrieval precision and preserved context, and why fixed-size chunking is a starting point rather than a final answer.
Explain what an embedding and vector similarity search compute conceptually, and when semantic search underperforms exact keyword matching.
Diagnose common RAG failure modes -- irrelevant retrieved chunks, ungrounded answers, boundary-cut context -- and identify which pipeline stage is responsible.
Explain why RAG substantially reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, tying the explanation back to the underlying generation mechanism.

sections.heading: The End-to-End Pipeline
sections.body:
RAG is best understood as a pipeline of independently tunable stages, and most real-world RAG debugging is really the work of isolating which specific stage is underperforming, rather than treating 'the RAG system' as one monolithic thing to fix. **Ingestion and chunking** splits source documents into passages small enough to be individually retrievable and to comfortably co-exist with several other chunks in a single prompt. **Embedding** converts each chunk's text into a dense numeric vector, produced by a separate embedding model, that's meant to capture the chunk's semantic content -- similar meanings should land at nearby points in that vector space. **Indexing** stores those vectors (usually alongside the original chunk text and metadata) in a structure -- often called a vector database or vector index -- built for fast nearest-neighbor search over potentially millions of vectors. **Retrieval** happens at query time: the incoming user query is embedded with the same embedding model, and the index is searched for the chunks whose vectors are most similar to the query's vector, returning the top-k matches. **Augmentation** inserts the text of those retrieved chunks directly into the prompt sent to the generation model, typically alongside explicit instructions about how to use them. **Generation** then produces the final answer, conditioned on both the original question and the injected context.

Each of these six stages can fail independently, and a poor final answer can trace back to any one of them -- bad chunking, a mismatched embedding model, a misconfigured index, a retrieval step returning irrelevant matches, weak augmentation instructions, or the generation model simply ignoring good context it was given. Treating RAG failures as 'the pipeline,' rather than immediately assuming the fix is always 'get a better generation model,' is the single most useful debugging habit for anyone building these systems.

sections.heading: Chunking: The Most Underrated Design Decision
sections.body:
Chunk size sits on a real, unavoidable tradeoff, and it's usually the first thing worth tuning when a RAG system underperforms. Chunks that are **too large** dilute the relevance signal used during retrieval -- a chunk containing one genuinely relevant sentence buried in several paragraphs of unrelated text gets an averaged, weaker similarity score than a tightly-relevant short chunk would, which can cause it to rank below chunks that are actually less useful; large chunks also mean fewer distinct chunks fit in your context budget, reducing how many different, independently-relevant pieces of information you can include per query. Chunks that are **too small**, on the other hand, lose the surrounding context a fragment needs to be individually meaningful -- a chunk containing just 'the deadline is March 3rd' with no sentence establishing what deadline is being discussed is close to useless once retrieved in isolation -- and they multiply the total number of vectors in your index, which increases both storage and retrieval latency.

**Overlap** between consecutive chunks (having each chunk share, say, the last 10-20% of its text with the next chunk) is the standard mitigation for the specific problem of an important sentence landing exactly on a chunk boundary and getting split across two chunks, neither of which contains the complete thought -- at the cost of some redundant storage. As a general practice, chunk boundaries that respect a document's natural structure (paragraph breaks, section headers) tend to outperform boundaries chosen purely by a fixed character or token count, because natural boundaries are more likely to also be semantic boundaries -- fixed-size chunking is a reasonable, simple starting point, not a technique to stop iterating on once it technically works.

sections.heading: Embeddings and Vector Similarity Search
sections.body:
An **embedding model** is a separate, typically much smaller model trained specifically to map a piece of text to a point in a high-dimensional vector space, such that text with similar meaning ends up at nearby points and text with different meaning ends up farther apart. Similarity between two vectors is usually measured with cosine similarity or a dot product, and 'retrieval' at query time is fundamentally the operation 'find the k stored vectors nearest to this query's vector.'

The practical power of this approach, relative to classic keyword search (like BM25 or a plain text index), is that it captures semantic relatedness rather than lexical overlap -- a query about 'automobile maintenance' can retrieve a chunk about 'car servicing' even though the two share almost no words in common, because an embedding model trained on enough text learns that those phrases mean similar things. But this comes with a real, often-underestimated cost: semantic search can genuinely underperform exact keyword matching for queries where the exact string matters -- a specific error code, a product SKU, a person's name, a precise legal term -- because two vectors can be semantically 'close' in a general sense while still failing to prioritize an exact match strongly enough, and the embedding model may not have learned fine-grained distinctions between similar-looking codes or identifiers it saw rarely (or never) during its own training. This is exactly why many production retrieval systems are **hybrid**: they combine semantic vector search with traditional keyword search (and often a separate reranking step that re-scores the combined candidate set with a more precise, more expensive model), rather than relying on embeddings alone.

sections.heading: Augmentation and Generation: Why Grounding Instructions Matter
sections.body:
Simply pasting retrieved chunk text into the prompt is not, on its own, enough to reliably ground the model's answer in it. The generation model still has its own trained-in knowledge conditioning every token alongside whatever text you've injected, and without explicit instruction, there's a genuine risk that the model blends the two, or in some cases favors its own (possibly outdated or simply wrong) trained-in belief over the retrieved text you actually wanted it to rely on. Explicit augmentation instructions -- 'answer only using the context provided below; if the answer is not contained in the context, say you don't know rather than guessing' -- meaningfully shift generation toward actually using the retrieved material as the primary source, rather than treating it as merely one more piece of loosely-relevant text sitting alongside everything else the model already 'knows.'

```python
system_prompt = (
    "Answer the user's question using ONLY the context below. "
    "If the answer is not present in the context, say you don't know -- "
    "do not use outside knowledge or guess.\n\nContext:\n" + retrieved_context
)
```

The two failure modes worth watching for are almost mirror images of each other: a model that ignores good, correctly-retrieved context in favor of its own prior belief (usually fixable with a firmer grounding instruction, and sometimes a lower temperature to reduce the chance of it drifting), and a model that answers confidently from context that was actually irrelevant because the retrieval step itself returned a poor match (which is a retrieval-stage bug, not something a better augmentation instruction can fix -- the model can't be grounded in relevant text it was never given).

sections.heading: Why RAG Reduces But Doesn't Eliminate Hallucination
sections.body:
RAG measurably reduces hallucination in practice, and the mechanism for why is straightforward given what you already know about generation: injecting relevant, verified text into the context narrows the space of plausible continuations toward content that's actually grounded in that text, the same way any other conditioning narrows the output space. This is genuinely one of the most effective hallucination mitigations available.

But generation is still the same underlying probabilistic mechanism as always, and RAG doesn't change that. If the retrieval stage returns irrelevant or wrong chunks, you've grounded the model in the wrong material, and it can still confidently generate an answer from that wrong material -- garbage in, confidently-phrased garbage out, from the model's point of view indistinguishable from the case where the retrieved material was actually correct. If the retrieved context is genuinely ambiguous or incomplete, the model may still fill gaps with its own trained-in assumptions rather than flagging the ambiguity. And even with good, relevant, unambiguous retrieved context, the model can still occasionally blend it with prior beliefs or misread a nuance in the source text. RAG changes the odds substantially in your favor -- it does not, and structurally cannot, reduce the underlying risk to exactly zero, because nothing about adding retrieved text changes the fact that the final answer is still produced token-by-token by the same mechanism covered in the previous module.

examples.title: A Minimal RAG Pipeline, Stage by Stage
examples.code:
def build_index(documents, chunk_size=500, overlap=50):
    chunks = []
    for doc in documents:
        chunks.extend(split_into_chunks(doc.text, chunk_size, overlap))
    vectors = [embed(chunk) for chunk in chunks]         # embedding stage
    return VectorIndex(vectors, chunks)                   # indexing stage

def answer_question(question, index, generation_model, top_k=4):
    query_vector = embed(question)
    retrieved = index.search(query_vector, top_k=top_k)   # retrieval stage
    context_text = "\n\n---\n\n".join(chunk.text for chunk in retrieved)
    prompt = (
        "Answer using ONLY the context below. If the answer isn't present, "
        "say you don't know.\n\nContext:\n" + context_text +
        "\n\nQuestion: " + question
    )
    return generation_model.generate(prompt)               # augmentation + generation stages

index = build_index(company_docs)
print(answer_question("What is the refund window for annual plans?", index, model))
examples.explanation: Each function call here maps directly onto one stage of the pipeline discussed in the explanation: `split_into_chunks` and `embed` inside `build_index` handle ingestion/chunking and embedding, `VectorIndex` handles indexing, `index.search` handles retrieval, and the prompt construction plus final `generation_model.generate` call handle augmentation and generation. When this pipeline gives a wrong or irrelevant answer, the debugging question is always 'which stage,' not 'is the model bad' -- print `retrieved` directly to check whether retrieval actually found relevant chunks before assuming the problem is in generation; inspect `chunks` right after `build_index` to check whether chunking produced sensible, self-contained passages; and only once retrieval is confirmed to be returning genuinely relevant material does it make sense to focus on the augmentation instructions or the generation model's behavior.

examples.title: Chunk Size Changes What Actually Gets Retrieved
examples.code:
source_paragraph = (
    "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of "
    "purchase. Monthly plan subscribers are not eligible for refunds but may "
    "cancel at any time to stop future charges. All refund requests must be "
    "submitted through the billing portal, not by email."
)

# Chunked as ONE large chunk (the whole paragraph):
# -> A query "how do monthly subscribers cancel" retrieves this whole chunk;
#    it contains the answer, but diluted alongside two unrelated refund rules.

# Chunked into THREE smaller, sentence-level chunks:
# -> chunk 1: "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase."
# -> chunk 2: "Monthly plan subscribers are not eligible for refunds but may cancel at any time to stop future charges."
# -> chunk 3: "All refund requests must be submitted through the billing portal, not by email."
# -> The same query now retrieves chunk 2 specifically, a tight, directly relevant match.
examples.explanation: This is a concrete illustration of the chunk-size tradeoff described in the explanation. The single large chunk isn't wrong, exactly -- the answer genuinely is present in it -- but it scores as a weaker, more diluted match during similarity search than a chunk that's purely about the topic the query asked about, because the embedding for the large chunk has to represent three different pieces of information averaged together. The smaller, sentence-level chunking produces a chunk whose embedding is almost entirely about the exact thing being asked, which tends to rank more highly and, once retrieved, gives the generation model a cleaner, more directly relevant piece of context to work from rather than needing to pick the right sentence back out of a larger, mixed passage. The tradeoff, not shown here, is that sentence-level chunks this small can lose broader context in other cases -- a real system typically lands somewhere between single-sentence and whole-document, tuned empirically against real queries.

examples.title: Grounding Instructions Change Whether Retrieved Context Actually Gets Used
examples.code:
retrieved_context = "Refunds for annual plans are available within 30 days of purchase."

weak_prompt = f"Context: {retrieved_context}\n\nQuestion: What is the refund policy?"

strong_prompt = (
    f"Answer the question using ONLY the context below. If the answer is not "
    f"in the context, say you don't know rather than guessing.\n\n"
    f"Context: {retrieved_context}\n\nQuestion: What is the refund policy?"
)
examples.explanation: Both prompts technically contain the same retrieved context, but they place very different conditioning pressure on how that context gets used. The weak version presents the context and the question side by side with no explicit instruction about their relationship -- the model is left to infer, on its own, how strictly it should stick to the provided text versus supplementing it with whatever general knowledge about refund policies it picked up during training, and different calls can resolve that ambiguity differently. The strong version explicitly instructs the model to treat the context as the sole source of truth and to explicitly decline rather than guess when the context is insufficient -- this measurably increases how consistently the model's answer traces back to the actual retrieved text rather than to an unrelated, generic assumption about how refund policies 'usually' work. Neither version guarantees perfect grounding -- the model can still occasionally deviate -- but the explicit instruction shifts the odds substantially, which is precisely why production RAG prompts almost always include this kind of explicit grounding instruction rather than presenting context passively.

misconceptions.description: Once RAG is added to a system, the model can no longer hallucinate, because it's effectively just looking up and returning the answer from a database rather than generating it.
misconceptions.clarification: RAG only changes what text is available in the context the model conditions on -- it does not change the fact that generation is still the same probabilistic, token-by-token mechanism as ever, drawing on both the injected context and the model's own trained-in knowledge. If retrieval returns irrelevant or wrong chunks, the model can still generate a confident, fluent, ungrounded answer from that bad material; if the retrieved context is ambiguous, the model can still fill the gap with an assumption rather than flagging uncertainty. RAG substantially reduces hallucination risk in practice, but it is a mitigation that shifts the odds, not a different, non-generative mechanism that makes fabrication structurally impossible.

misconceptions.description: Bigger chunks -- or feeding whole documents instead of chunking at all -- are always better, because the model has 'more context to work with.'
misconceptions.clarification: Larger chunks dilute the relevance signal that similarity search relies on: a long chunk containing one relevant sentence amid several irrelevant ones scores as a weaker match than a short chunk that's tightly about the query topic, which can cause genuinely useful material to rank below less useful material during retrieval. Larger chunks also mean fewer distinct, independently-relevant pieces of information fit within your context budget for a given query. There's a real design tradeoff between chunk size and both retrieval precision and preserved surrounding context -- it isn't a monotonic 'bigger is better' relationship in either direction.

exercises.prompt: This RAG function retrieves relevant chunks but the model's answers never actually reflect the retrieved content -- they read like generic, ungrounded responses. Find the bug.
hints: Trace `context_text` after it's built -- is it actually included anywhere in the string that gets sent to `generation_model.generate`?

Retrieval can be working perfectly (returning genuinely relevant chunks) while augmentation -- the step that's supposed to inject those chunks into the prompt -- silently fails to do so. Check which stage this bug actually lives in.
The fix isn't about retrieval quality at all here -- it's about actually including `context_text` inside the `prompt` string, along with an instruction telling the model to use it.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The retrieval stage is working exactly as intended -- `retrieved` and `context_text` are correctly computed -- but the augmentation stage never actually happens: `context_text` is built and then simply discarded, since the `prompt` sent to the model only contains the raw question. This is a good example of why RAG debugging should isolate stages: it's tempting to assume 'ungrounded answers' means a generation-model or retrieval-quality problem, but here the entire pipeline up through retrieval is fine, and the bug is specifically that the augmentation step -- inserting retrieved text into the prompt -- was never wired up. The fix interpolates `context_text` into the prompt and adds an explicit grounding instruction, which is what actually gives the generation model something to be grounded in.

exercises.prompt: A RAG system retrieves the top 10 chunks for every query with no similarity-score filtering, and it's returning several barely-related chunks alongside the genuinely relevant ones, diluting the context with noise. Write a function filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score) that takes a list of (chunk, similarity_score) tuples and returns only the chunks meeting a minimum similarity threshold, preserving their original relative order.
exercises.code:
def filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score):
    # retrieved_chunks: list of (chunk_text, similarity_score) tuples, already sorted by score descending
    # return: list of chunk_text strings whose similarity_score >= min_score
    pass
hints: This doesn't require re-sorting anything -- the input is already described as sorted by score descending, so a simple filter that preserves order is sufficient.
Watch the off-by-one direction on the comparison: you want to KEEP chunks whose score is at or above the threshold, not strictly above it.
The return type should be a list of just the chunk text strings, not the (chunk, score) tuples -- make sure you're unpacking correctly.
exercises.solutionCode:
def filter_by_relevance(retrieved_chunks, min_score):
    return [chunk for chunk, score in retrieved_chunks if score >= min_score]

# Example:
retrieved = [("Refunds for annual plans...", 0.91), ("Our office hours are...", 0.42), ("Monthly plans cannot be refunded...", 0.86)]
print(filter_by_relevance(retrieved, min_score=0.75))
# ['Refunds for annual plans...', 'Monthly plans cannot be refunded...']
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is a small but genuinely important production pattern: raw top-k retrieval always returns exactly k results regardless of whether all k are actually relevant, because 'top-k' just means 'the k best matches available,' not 'the matches that are actually good.' A simple similarity-score threshold, applied after retrieval and before augmentation, filters out chunks that only barely resemble the query -- if a query has fewer than k genuinely relevant chunks in the index, this correctly returns fewer than k chunks (or even zero) rather than padding the context with noise just to hit a fixed count. In a real system, `min_score` itself typically needs empirical tuning against a set of representative queries, since the 'right' threshold depends heavily on which embedding model produced the scores and how your specific corpus is distributed in that vector space.

assessments.prompt: A support bot using RAG confidently answers a question with information that sounds plausible but is actually about an unrelated product from the indexed documents. Retrieval logs show the top-k chunks it was given were all genuinely about that unrelated product. Which stage of the pipeline is the most likely root cause?
options: The generation model, which should be replaced with a larger model.
The retrieval stage -- the query embedding matched chunks that were not actually relevant to the user's question.
The augmentation stage, because grounding instructions can't fix irrelevant retrieved content in the first place.
The tokenizer, which likely mis-split the user's question.
assessments.explanation: Given that the logs confirm the retrieved chunks themselves were about the wrong product, the model did exactly what a well-grounded generation step should do: it answered based on the context it was actually given. The failure happened earlier, in retrieval, which returned the wrong chunks in the first place -- no amount of good generation-model behavior or well-written grounding instructions can produce a correct answer from context that's fundamentally about the wrong topic. Option A misdiagnoses a retrieval problem as a generation-capability problem. Option C is a reasonable-sounding but incorrect claim -- augmentation instructions govern how retrieved context is used, not whether the right context was retrieved to begin with, so it's not the root cause here (though it's true they can't fix it after the fact). Option D is implausible on the evidence given; nothing here points to a tokenization failure.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a RAG-based chatbot might confidently give a wrong answer to a question even though the correct information genuinely exists somewhere in the indexed document set, walking through where in the pipeline this could go wrong.
assessments.modelAnswer: The correct information existing somewhere in the indexed corpus only helps if every subsequent stage of the pipeline successfully carries it through to the final answer, and there are several independent points where that chain can break. The problem could originate in chunking, if the correct information was split awkwardly across a chunk boundary, leaving no single chunk that contains the complete, coherent answer, or if it was embedded inside a large chunk dominated by unrelated content, weakening its similarity score. It could originate in retrieval itself, if the query's embedding simply doesn't land close enough to the correct chunk's embedding in vector space -- this happens especially often when the question uses very different wording or terminology than the source document, or when the answer depends on an exact match (an ID, a specific term) that semantic similarity search handles less reliably than keyword search would. It could originate in augmentation, if the retrieved chunks are actually correct but the prompt doesn't include a firm enough grounding instruction, leaving room for the model to blend in its own unrelated trained-in assumptions rather than sticking strictly to what was retrieved. And even if retrieval and augmentation both worked perfectly, the failure could still originate in generation itself, since the model is still producing its answer through ordinary next-token prediction and can occasionally misread, oversimplify, or blend a nuance of the correct retrieved text with something else. Diagnosing which of these actually happened requires inspecting the pipeline at each stage rather than guessing -- checking what was actually retrieved for the failing query is usually the fastest and highest-value first step, since a large fraction of real-world RAG failures turn out to be retrieval failures rather than generation failures.

concepts.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs Prompting: Choosing the Right Tool
concepts.description: Fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting change three different things -- model weights, available context, and per-call instructions, respectively -- and confusing which lever actually addresses your problem leads teams to fine-tune away a knowledge problem that RAG would have solved in an afternoon, or to prompt-engineer around a behavior gap that only real training data can close.
learningObjectives: Distinguish what fine-tuning changes (model weights and default behavior) from what RAG changes (available context per call) and what prompting changes (per-call instructions).
Classify a given problem as primarily a knowledge problem, a behavior/format problem, or a specification problem, and match it to the right tool.
Explain the cost, latency, and maintenance tradeoffs across prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning.
Explain why fine-tuning is a poor fix for factual or frequently-changing knowledge, and why RAG is a poor fix for consistent style, tone, or format shifts.
Design a layered strategy for a realistic product scenario that combines prompting and RAG first, reaching for fine-tuning only when justified by data and scale.

sections.heading: Three Different Levers for Three Different Problems
sections.body:
It's worth stating this precisely, because the three techniques are extremely easy to conflate in casual conversation despite doing genuinely different things. **Prompting** changes per-call instructions -- it's the cheapest and fastest to iterate on, changes nothing persistent about the model, and every effect disappears the moment you stop including that instruction in the request. **RAG** changes what's available in the context for a given call, by retrieving and injecting external, often frequently-changing or private information at inference time -- it also changes nothing about the model's weights or its default behavior; it just gives the model different material to condition on. **Fine-tuning** is additional training that actually adjusts the model's weights, which persistently shifts its default behavior, tone, or narrow-task performance without needing to repeat an instruction on every call.

The most important consequence of this distinction: these are not, in most real situations, three competing solutions to the same problem that you pick between based on preference or budget. They answer three different questions -- 'what do I want the model to know for this specific call' (RAG), 'what do I want to tell it to do right now' (prompting), and 'what do I want it to always, persistently do or be good at, without being told again each time' (fine-tuning). Treating them as interchangeable is the root of most of the mismatched-tool mistakes covered in the rest of this concept.

sections.heading: When Fine-Tuning Is the Right Tool
sections.body:
Fine-tuning earns its cost and complexity in a few genuine, recurring situations. First, when you need a specific output format or style reproduced extremely consistently across a very high volume of calls, and maintaining that consistency via a long instruction-plus-few-shot-examples block in every single prompt is itself becoming a real cost -- fine-tuning bakes the pattern into the weights, so the prompt no longer needs to re-explain or re-demonstrate it every time, saving real tokens (and therefore cost and latency) at scale. Second, when you're teaching a narrow behavior or classification boundary that's genuinely hard to specify precisely in words but easy to demonstrate with a large number of labeled examples -- a subtle tone distinction, a nuanced categorization task with many edge cases -- where the sheer volume of examples needed exceeds what's practical to fit as few-shot examples in a single prompt. Third, when the base model handles your actual input distribution poorly -- heavy domain-specific jargon, an unusual input format, a language variety the base model wasn't trained on much -- and no amount of prompting closes that gap because the limitation is in the model's underlying representations, not in what it's been told to do with them.

Each of these comes with real prerequisites and costs worth being honest about: you need a reasonably large, high-quality, genuinely representative labeled dataset (a small or biased dataset produces a correspondingly narrow or biased fine-tune); the iteration loop is slow and expensive relative to editing a prompt, since retraining takes real time and money, and evaluating whether a new fine-tune actually improved things (without silently degrading other capabilities) takes real effort; and a poorly executed fine-tune can cause the model to regress on tasks it previously handled fine, sometimes called catastrophic forgetting -- fine-tuning is not a low-risk, low-cost lever the way changing a prompt is.

sections.heading: When Fine-Tuning Is the Wrong Tool
sections.body:
The single most common fine-tuning misapplication, by a wide margin, is using it to try to inject **knowledge** -- facts, current data, a company's internal documentation -- into a model, in the hope that it will then reliably 'know' and recall that information on demand. This doesn't work the way people expect, for a specific mechanical reason: fine-tuning adjusts weights in a diffuse, statistical way across the whole training process, and it is not a reliable mechanism for a model to recall a specific fact verbatim, on demand, especially one that appeared only a handful of times in the fine-tuning data. The exact same probabilistic generation mechanism that causes hallucination in the base model governs what a fine-tuned model produces too -- fine-tuning shifts the probability distribution, it doesn't install a lookup table, so a fine-tuned model can just as easily paraphrase, blend, or simply forget a specific fine-tuned fact as recall it precisely.

On top of that reliability problem, there's a freshness and traceability problem that's arguably worse in practice: any fact baked into fine-tuning weights becomes stale the moment the real-world information changes, and un-staling it requires another full retraining cycle -- slow and expensive compared to simply re-indexing an updated document for RAG, which can happen in minutes. And a fine-tuned model's answer, even when correct, offers no natural way to show *which specific source* it came from, whereas a RAG answer can point directly at the retrieved passage that supports it. For essentially any 'the model needs to know X' requirement where X is factual, sourced, or subject to change over time, RAG is both the cheaper and the more reliable, more traceable tool -- and this holds even when budget for fine-tuning genuinely isn't a constraint, because the limitation is mechanical, not financial.

sections.heading: The Decision in Practice: A Simple Heuristic
sections.body:
A practical decision heuristic, worth running through explicitly before committing engineering effort to any one approach: if the core problem is 'the model doesn't know something,' 'this information changes regularly,' or 'we need to be able to trace an answer back to a source,' that's a knowledge problem, and RAG is the right lever, essentially regardless of budget. If the core problem is 'the model does know how to do this, but I need it to consistently behave a specific way on every single call, re-explaining that behavior every time is expensive or produces inconsistent results, and we have a large, clean set of examples of exactly the behavior we want,' that's a genuine fine-tuning candidate -- but it's still worth trying prompting and few-shot examples first, since they're nearly free to test and often close enough of the gap that fine-tuning turns out to be unnecessary. If the core problem is 'I just need to phrase this one feature's instructions more precisely, or show a couple of examples of the format I want,' that's a prompting problem, full stop, and reaching for RAG or fine-tuning would be solving a problem you don't actually have.

In practice, most real systems layer these: start with prompting because it's essentially free to iterate on, add RAG once there's a genuine knowledge, freshness, or traceability need, and only reach for fine-tuning once prompting and RAG together have demonstrably hit a ceiling on a specific, reproducible behavior gap, and there's a real labeled dataset available to fine-tune on -- fine-tuning as a first move, before establishing that the first two levers are insufficient, is very often solving the wrong problem, or solving the right problem with the most expensive and slowest available tool.

sections.heading: A Layered Example
sections.body:
Consider an internal support-ticket triage assistant that needs to categorize incoming tickets, cite the relevant internal policy for its categorization decision, and output a consistent structured format for downstream automation. The layered build-out looks like this: start with **prompting** -- a clear system instruction describing the categories, the required output schema, and a couple of few-shot examples of well-formed classifications; this alone often gets a working first version. Add **RAG** once it's clear the assistant needs to reference actual, current internal policy documents to justify its categorization and those documents change periodically -- retrieving the relevant policy section per ticket and citing it directly solves both the knowledge-freshness problem and the traceability requirement, and it does so without ever touching model weights.

Only later, if ticket volume is high enough that the per-call cost of the few-shot examples and lengthy schema instructions becomes a meaningful expense, and there's by then a large, clean dataset of human-verified correct classifications accumulated from production traffic, would fine-tuning become worth considering -- specifically to bake in the consistent output-formatting behavior (which doesn't change over time) so it no longer needs to be re-specified in every prompt, while the retrieval step keeps handling the policy knowledge (which does change over time) exactly as before. Fine-tuning the formatting behavior while keeping RAG for the knowledge is a good illustration of the core principle: the two techniques solve different halves of the same system, and neither one should be asked to solve the half it's mechanically ill-suited for.

examples.title: The Wrong-Tool Attempt: Fine-Tuning on Policy Text
examples.code:
# Attempt: fine-tune a model on a dataset built from the company's internal
# policy documents, hoping it will then reliably answer policy questions
# and cite the right policy.

training_examples = [
    {"prompt": "What is the refund window for annual plans?",
     "completion": "Annual plan subscribers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase, per Section 4.2 of the Refund Policy."},
    # ... hundreds more examples generated from policy documents ...
]

# fine_tune(base_model, training_examples)  -- weeks later, in production:
# The policy changes (30 days -> 45 days). The fine-tuned model keeps
# confidently citing "30 days" and "Section 4.2" until it is retrained
# on an updated dataset -- a slow, costly cycle to repeat every time policy changes.
examples.explanation: This looks reasonable on paper -- there's real training data, and the model probably will learn to answer *some* policy questions correctly right after fine-tuning. The failure shows up over time and under pressure: the moment the actual policy changes, the fine-tuned model has no way to know that, because the fact is baked statistically into its weights rather than looked up fresh each time, and it will keep confidently, fluently citing outdated information -- with a specific fabricated-sounding section reference that adds false credibility -- until someone notices, rebuilds the training dataset, and pays for another full fine-tuning run. This is precisely the knowledge-freshness and traceability problem described in the explanation: the fix isn't a better fine-tuning dataset, it's recognizing that factual, changeable information belongs in a retrieval index that can be updated in minutes, not in model weights that can only be updated through a full retraining cycle.

examples.title: A Case Where Fine-Tuning Actually Wins
examples.code:
# A classification pipeline processes 2 million support tickets per month.
# The current prompt includes a lengthy instruction block plus 8 few-shot
# examples to enforce a specific, consistent structured-output format --
# roughly 900 extra tokens on EVERY single call, purely to establish format
# and tone, which never actually changes ticket to ticket.

cost_per_1k_tokens = 0.01
extra_tokens_per_call = 900
calls_per_month = 2_000_000

monthly_cost_of_repeated_instructions = (
    extra_tokens_per_call / 1000 * cost_per_1k_tokens * calls_per_month
)
print(monthly_cost_of_repeated_instructions)   # roughly $18,000/month, just for repeated formatting instructions

# There is also a large (50,000+), clean, human-verified dataset of past
# correctly-classified tickets available from production history -- and the
# desired formatting behavior itself doesn't change over time.
examples.explanation: This is close to the ideal fine-tuning scenario: the behavior being reinforced is stable over time (the output format and tone aren't expected to change), it's currently being re-specified at real, recurring cost on every single call, and there's a large, high-quality, representative labeled dataset already sitting in production history rather than needing to be manually constructed. Fine-tuning on that existing dataset could let the ~900 tokens of formatting instruction and examples be removed from every call entirely, directly cutting the $18,000/month figure (plus reducing latency, since shorter prompts also process faster) while likely improving format consistency, since the behavior is now baked into the model's default output rather than depending on the model correctly following instructions every single time. Note what's *not* being fine-tuned here -- the actual category definitions and any policy content the ticket classification might reference are exactly the kind of knowledge that should keep coming from RAG or an explicit prompt, not get folded into this same fine-tune.

examples.title: A Decision Function Encoding the Heuristic
examples.explanation: This deliberately simplified function encodes the heuristic from the explanation as an explicit, checkable priority order rather than a vague feeling: knowledge-freshness and citation needs are checked first and route straight to RAG regardless of anything else, because no amount of stable, high-volume behavior or good training data changes the fact that fine-tuning is structurally unreliable for exactly those two needs. Only once those are ruled out does the function even consider fine-tuning, and even then only when both a genuine need for consistent narrow behavior *and* a large labeled dataset are present together -- missing either one falls through to plain prompting, which matches the real-world guidance that prompting is always worth trying first regardless of what this function returns, since it's essentially free to test before committing to a fine-tuning project. A real decision would weigh cost, volume, and team capacity too, but the ordering of checks -- knowledge needs before behavior-consistency needs, and both before defaulting to prompting -- captures the core of the reasoning.

misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning is the more advanced, more powerful version of prompting or RAG, so given enough budget, it's always the strongest choice available.
misconceptions.clarification: Fine-tuning, RAG, and prompting are different levers that change different things -- weights, available context, and per-call instructions, respectively -- not a ladder of increasing power where fine-tuning sits at the top. Fine-tuning is actually the wrong, less reliable, and more expensive tool for knowledge and freshness problems, where RAG is both cheaper and structurally better suited, regardless of how much budget is available. 'More advanced' and 'more appropriate for this specific problem' are different things, and treating fine-tuning as a universal upgrade leads directly to using it for exactly the problems it handles worst.

misconceptions.description: The right way to make a model 'know' a company's product or internal documentation is to fine-tune it on that documentation.
misconceptions.clarification: This is the single most common fine-tuning misapplication. Fine-tuning does not give a model reliable, verbatim, on-demand recall of specific facts -- it adjusts weights diffusely across training, and the resulting model can paraphrase, blend, or simply forget specific fine-tuned facts, governed by the same probabilistic mechanism that produces hallucination generally. It also makes answers harder to trace back to a specific source, and makes the knowledge stale the moment the real documentation changes, requiring a full retraining cycle to fix. Retrieval-augmented generation addresses this exact need -- a model 'knowing' current, specific, sourced information -- far more directly, cheaply, and reliably, by retrieving the actual relevant text at query time rather than trying to compress it into model weights.

exercises.prompt: Write a function choose_approach(problem: dict) -> str that returns 'rag', 'fine-tuning', or 'prompting' given a dict with boolean keys: knowledge_changes_frequently, needs_source_citation, needs_consistent_narrow_behavior_at_scale, has_large_labeled_dataset. Follow this priority: if the knowledge changes frequently OR needs source citation, choose RAG. Otherwise, if consistent narrow behavior at scale is needed AND a large labeled dataset exists, choose fine-tuning. Otherwise, default to prompting.
hints: Check the RAG conditions first, using `or` between the two knowledge/citation flags -- either one alone should be enough to route to RAG.
Only after ruling out the RAG conditions should you check the fine-tuning conditions, and that check needs `and`, not `or` -- both a genuine need AND a dataset must be present.
Make sure there's a final fallback branch that returns 'prompting' when neither of the earlier conditions matched -- this is the default, not a case you should ever need to raise an error for.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The ordering here is doing the real work, not just the boolean logic: RAG is checked first and with `or`, because either a freshness need or a citation need on its own is sufficient reason to avoid fine-tuning entirely, regardless of anything else about the problem -- fine-tuning is structurally unsuited to both needs no matter how much other evidence points toward it. The fine-tuning branch is checked second and with `and`, because fine-tuning should only be chosen when both a genuine, high-volume behavior-consistency need exists AND there's real data to train on -- having just one without the other (a behavior need with no dataset, or a dataset with no real need for consistency at scale) should fall through to prompting instead, which is the safe, cheap default when neither of the stronger conditions clearly applies.

exercises.prompt: A team fine-tunes their support assistant every single night on that day's current product pricing, hoping to keep it 'up to date.' This is expensive, slow to deploy (each nightly fine-tune takes hours), and the assistant is still occasionally caught quoting stale prices from earlier in the day when prices changed intraday. Identify the architectural mistake and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
# nightly_job.py (runs once per day, roughly 2am)
def nightly_retrain():
    current_pricing_data = fetch_current_pricing()
    training_examples = build_training_examples(current_pricing_data)
    fine_tune(base_model="support-assistant-v3", examples=training_examples)
    deploy_new_model_version()   # takes several hours end-to-end
hints: Pricing is described as changing 'intraday' -- how does that compare to the frequency of this fix, which only runs once per night?

This is the same fine-tuning-for-knowledge mismatch covered in the explanation, just applied to pricing instead of policy text -- what's the mechanical reason fine-tuning struggles here regardless of how often you run it?
Consider what it would take to make pricing information update in near-real-time instead of on a slow, expensive nightly training cycle.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Replace nightly fine-tuning of pricing with a retrieval-backed index that
# updates the moment pricing changes, and inject the current price directly
# into the prompt at query time.

def on_pricing_change(updated_pricing_data):
    update_pricing_index(updated_pricing_data)   # near-instant, no retraining

def answer_pricing_question(question, pricing_index, generation_model):
    relevant_pricing = pricing_index.search(embed(question), top_k=3)
    context = "\n".join(p.text for p in relevant_pricing)
    prompt = (
        "Answer using ONLY the current pricing information below. "
        "If the answer isn't present, say you don't know.\n\n"
        f"Current pricing:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
    )
    return generation_model.generate(prompt)
exercises.solutionExplanation: The architectural mistake is using fine-tuning -- a slow, expensive, batch process -- to try to keep the assistant current on exactly the kind of information most likely to change faster than the fine-tuning cycle can keep up with. Even running it nightly, any intraday price change is stale until the next 2am run, and the underlying mechanism has the same reliability problem covered in the explanation regardless of frequency: fine-tuning doesn't give the model a precise, verbatim lookup for a specific number, so even freshly-retrained pricing knowledge is a probabilistic approximation, not a guarantee. The fix replaces nightly retraining with a retrieval index that updates the moment pricing actually changes (a near-instant operation, nothing like a multi-hour training run) and injects the current, correct price directly into the prompt at the moment a pricing question is asked -- this is both more current (updates in near-real-time rather than once a day) and structurally more reliable (the exact price is present as text in the context, rather than approximated from training).

assessments.prompt: A team wants their support bot to always answer questions using the current version of their refund policy, which changes every few weeks. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Fine-tune the model on the refund policy text every time it changes.
Use retrieval-augmented generation over an index of the current policy document, updated whenever the policy changes.
Increase the model's temperature so it is more likely to guess the updated policy correctly.
Lengthen the system prompt with a general reminder to 'always be accurate about refund policy.'
assessments.explanation: This is a knowledge-freshness problem -- specific factual content that changes on a regular cadence -- which is exactly the category RAG is suited for: updating a retrieval index when the policy changes is fast and cheap, and it keeps the model's answers traceable to the actual current document. Option A repeats the classic fine-tuning-for-knowledge mistake -- it's slow, expensive to repeat every few weeks, and fine-tuning doesn't reliably store an exact, verbatim, retrievable version of the policy text anyway. Option C is unrelated to the actual problem -- temperature governs sampling randomness, not access to correct information, and would if anything make answers less consistent, not more accurate. Option D fails for the same reason a generic 'answer accurately' instruction always fails: telling the model to be accurate about content it was never actually given access to doesn't create that access.

assessments.prompt: A product manager asks: 'Can't we just fine-tune the model on all our documentation so it knows everything, and skip building this complicated retrieval system?' Explain, in terms a PM without a technical background could follow, why this wouldn't work as well as they expect, and what you'd propose instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning is a way of adjusting the model through additional training so its default behavior shifts -- it's genuinely good at teaching a consistent style, tone, or way of formatting answers. But it turns out to be a surprisingly unreliable way to make a model 'know' specific facts on demand, for a concrete reason: the training process spreads what it learns across the model's internal parameters in a diffuse, statistical way, rather than storing anything like an exact, lookup-able copy of the original documents. In practice, that means a model fine-tuned on documentation can still get specific details wrong, blend information from different documents together, or simply not reliably reproduce a fact it only saw a handful of times during training -- the same underlying tendency that causes a model to occasionally state something confidently and incorrectly in general also applies to information baked in through fine-tuning. On top of that reliability gap, there are two more practical problems: whenever the documentation changes -- and documentation changes constantly -- the fine-tuned model doesn't automatically know about the update; it needs to go through another full, slow, and costly retraining cycle before it reflects the new information, whereas updating a retrieval-based system is closer to instant. And if a fine-tuned answer is wrong, there's no natural way to point at exactly which document it came from to check it, whereas a retrieval-based answer can show the exact passage it used, which matters a lot for trust and for catching mistakes. What I'd propose instead is retrieval-augmented generation: rather than trying to compress the documentation into the model's training, we keep the documentation as-is, searchable, and at the moment someone asks a question, we automatically find the specific relevant passages and hand them to the model along with the question, so it answers from the actual current text rather than from a fuzzy training-time memory of it. This ends up being cheaper to keep up to date, easier to verify, and in practice more accurate for exactly the kind of 'does the model know our documentation' need the fine-tuning idea was trying to solve.
